1:
Whether the denial in the third verse is absolute or comparative divides them at once. Clarke settles it by supplying two words in brackets: not with our fathers only, but with us also. Ellicott gives the grammatical warrant, that this is the usage of the Hebrew in drawing contrasts, so the meaning is not only with our fathers but with us also, who were in their loins; and he adds a calculation nobody else makes, that every man above forty-two at the time of this discourse might actually remember the day at Sinai. Wesley reaches the same sense another way: Moses does not say that all who made the covenant at Sinai are now alive, but that it was made with all who are now alive, since it was made with the elders in their persons and the rest in their parents. Gill takes it as not with them only, on the authority of three Jewish commentators, since the law was certainly given to the immediate fathers of this generation.

Keil reads the denial as a real exclusion, and must say who is excluded — which produces the sharpest disagreement here, since he names the men he rejects. The fathers are neither those who died in the wilderness, as Augustine supposed, nor the forefathers in Egypt, as Calvin imagined, but the patriarchs. Henry reaches the same answer and gives the reason Keil does not: the covenant was not made with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, since to them God gave the covenant of circumcision and not that of the ten commandments, the light of revelation shining gradually so that the children knew more than their fathers had. Gill allows this as the alternative to his own, observing that if the remote ancestors are meant, the covenant of grace made with them was one thing and the law delivered four hundred and thirty years later another.

Face to face divides them again, and along a different line. Calvin takes the phrase in its warmest sense, as equivalent to discoursing openly and familiarly, and says that in point of fact God spoke with them as mortals and friends communicate; Wesley agrees, glossing it personally and immediately, freely and familiarly, so as not to overwhelm and confound them. Keil denies precisely that. The Hebrew phrase here is not the one used of God speaking to Moses, which expresses the very confidential relation in which the Lord spoke to him as one friend to another; this one denotes only the directness with which Jehovah spoke to the people, that he came as near to them as one person to another. Gill takes the same line: it does not mean the free and familiar manner in which he talked with Moses, but that he spoke publicly and distinctly without a middle person. Henry keeps the openness without the friendship, rendering it word to word after the Chaldee and contrasting it with the dark visions of old.

Two of them use the passage for more than exposition. Henry finds in it the condescension of divine grace, which turns a command into a covenant so that we may be the more strongly bound by our own consent and the more encouraged by the divine promise; and he takes the mediator standing at the foot of the mount as a type of Christ, who stands between God and man as one that has laid his hand upon both, so that we may hear from God and speak to him without trembling. Clarke turns the first verse into a ladder of five steps: God speaks; the people are called to hear; to learn what they heard; to keep God's testimonies in mind and treasure them in an upright heart; and to do them, taking his word for the invariable rule of their conduct. Should not all these points, he asks, be kept in view by every Christian assembly?
6:
Henry begins with the repetition: though they had been spoken before and written, they are again rehearsed, for precept must be upon precept and line upon line, and all little enough to keep the word of God in our minds. He notes some variation from the earlier record, compares the two forms in which the Lord's prayer has come down to us, and draws the rule that we must tie ourselves to the things rather than to the words unalterably. Gill says the same more briefly, that the commands are delivered in the same order and nearly the same words; on the sabbath he marks a small difference, that the text here says keep the sabbath day where the earlier place says remember it, the institution having been made before. Ellicott takes the commandments word by word. Before me is literally upon my face, in addition to my presence — idols being at best only masks which man puts upon the face of God, insulting to his dignity and tending to conceal him from view. Taking the name in vain is literally putting the name of Jehovah thy God to vanity, that is, to anything false or hollow or unreal; false swearing is primarily forbidden, but the extension of the principle to rash swearing, or the light use of the Name without real cause, is obvious enough.

Calvin spends most of his comment closing an escape route. Idolaters endeavour in vain to elude the second commandment by distinguishing two kinds of honour, reserving the higher for God and paying the lesser to pictures and statues; but Moses first comprehends all the forms and ceremonies of worship and then adds the word which properly means to serve, so the evasion is childish. And even granting the distinction they do not escape, since the prohibition amounts to God's declaring that he will not be worshipped in wood and stone or any other likeness.

The visiting of iniquity is the hard verse, and Calvin states the difficulty before answering. Nothing is more unreasonable than that the innocent and the guilty should be involved in the same punishment, and the prophet's declaration is well known, that the soul that sinneth shall die. He answers that the prophet was refuting a false complaint, since not one of those with whom God was severe was free from crime; and that he is at liberty to punish the crimes of the fathers upon their descendants, with the proviso that these too may be justly punished as imitators. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion in two sentences: it is not meant that the soul of the son shall die for the father, the penalty extending only to them that hate God; and no sins so surely entail consequences on later generations as the abominations of idolatry.

On the promise of mercy they converge again. Calvin will not let it be read as a debt: God does not say he will be faithful or just towards the keepers of his law but merciful. What he does find is a disproportion he thinks decisive: God limits his vengeance to the third or fourth generation and extends his mercy to a thousand, so that he plainly prefers to attract men by gentle invitations rather than extort obedience by threatenings. Wesley turns the whole into examination. Has the reader worshipped God in spirit and in truth, and sought no happiness besides the knowledge and love of God? If not, thou hast other gods before him. Has he used the name of God only on solemn occasions, and then with the deepest awe, looking on heaven as God's throne and earth as his footstool and every creature as full of God? Does he on the sabbath do no work that could be done as well on another day, and watch narrowly over all within his gates, that they too may keep it holy?
14:
The most considerable variation falls in the fourth commandment, and Henry and Clarke account for it differently. Henry observes that in Exodus the reason annexed is taken from the creation of the world and here from the deliverance out of Egypt, and explains the change: that deliverance was typical of our redemption by Jesus Christ, in remembrance of which the Christian sabbath was to be observed. Clarke does not choose between the reasons but counts them, finding three grand ends in the appointment: to commemorate the creation; to give a due proportion of rest to man and beast, since in Egypt they had none, so that having shown them mercy God teaches them to show it to their servants; and to afford spiritual advantages, keeping the soul in remembrance of the rest which remains. He adds an explanation nobody else offers for a smaller variation, that the sabbath day stands here where the earlier text has the seventh, which he takes to be owing to a change of the day at the exodus, from Sunday to Saturday, effected upon the gathering of the manna — so the sabbath became a twofold memorial, which accounts for the new reason assigned.

Two of them notice the same feature in what follows and draw the same inference. Henry observes that the last five commandments are coupled together here, which they are not in Exodus — neither shalt thou commit adultery, neither shalt thou steal — and takes this to intimate that God's commands are all of a piece, the same authority that obliges us to one obliging us to another, so that we must not be partial in the law, for he that offends in one point is guilty of all. Gill notices the same conjunctions, that these commands begin with the copulative and, differently from the earlier place, which joins them together and to what precedes; hence, he says, the law is by some said to be one copulative. On the fifth commandment three of them converge. Henry marks the addition of the words that it may go well with thee, which the apostle quotes and puts first; and he meets the difficulty it raises, that if some have been dutiful to their parents and yet not lived long, the promise may be reconciled thus — whether they live long or not, it shall go well with them, in this world or a better. Ellicott notes only that it is in this form that Paul cites the commandment; Gill that it is the first commandment with promise, the promise being of long life and happiness in the land.

Wesley does something none of the others attempt. Observing that little had been said about the spiritual sense of the ten commandments where they were first given, he adds a few questions here which the reader may answer between God and his own soul, and runs them through commandment by commandment. On honouring parents he asks whether the reader has slighted their advice, supplied their wants, concealed their infirmities, and whether servants have done all things as unto Christ, not with eye-service but in singleness of heart. On the sixth he presses the commandment far past killing: have you tempted any one to what might shorten his life, or suffered intemperance under your roof; are you guilty of no degree of self-murder, and do you never eat or drink anything merely because you like it when you believe it prejudicial to your health; and have you not hated your neighbour in your heart, since if you failed to reprove him that sinned in your sight, you have in God's account hated him. Ellicott, on the tenth commandment, notices that where the earlier text employs one verb this employs two, the idea of the one being to delight in and the other to lust after; Gill takes lust to be the thing intended.
22:
What is meant by God's adding no more divides them three ways. Calvin takes it as a statement of sufficiency: a perfect rule of life is contained in the ten commandments, so that when their instruction is fully received the whole body of wisdom is attained and the people need seek no more — when God made an end of speaking, he himself laid down the bounds of legitimate inquiry. Henry takes the same sense and turns it into a prohibition: other laws were sent by Moses, but no more were spoken in that manner, and since he added no more we must not add, for the law of the Lord is perfect. Wesley reads it not as sufficiency but as a change of mode: God ceased for that time to speak immediately and with that loud voice, the rest being delivered to Moses and communicated by him; and this he did to show the preeminence of that law above the rest, and its everlasting obligation.

The people's own words then produce Calvin's closest piece of reading. When they confess that they saw the glory and the greatness of God, he says, they oblige themselves to obedience unless they choose avowedly to make war against him; and when they add that God doth talk with man and he liveth, they are expressing astonishment at what was scarcely to be believed, since a long period had elapsed since such revelations ceased and they are amazed as at a new thing. Then he notices an apparent inconsistency: the two following verses seem to contradict each other, for having found that those to whom God manifests himself are not always destroyed, why say they shall die if he continues to speak? His answer is that they fear for the future the danger they had escaped by a marvellous indulgence: it is as if they had said that it is more than enough once to have provoked God against us, and of his inestimable loving-kindness that he has thus far pardoned us, so that we must beware lest our perversity bring heavier punishment. Gill takes the same clauses more simply, giving one Jewish commentator's division: the glory means the appearance of fire in which the Lord was, the greatness the thunders and lightnings and the voice of the trumpet.

On the request for a mediator, Henry and Calvin draw the same lesson from opposite ends. Henry lists what may be inferred from the request: that they expected further commands and were willing to hear more; that they thought Moses able to bear discoveries of the divine glory under which they knew themselves unable to stand; and that they were for the moment in a good mind under strong convictions of what they had heard. He adds two cautions. They believed Moses a favourite of Heaven and one who would be faithful to them, yet at other times they murmured at him and a little before this were ready to stone him — see how men's convictions correct their passions. And many have their consciences startled by the law who have them not purified, fair promises being extorted from them but no good principles fixed and rooted. Calvin turns the episode against a temptation of his own day: since the experience of God's ancient people ought to persuade us that when he sets teachers over us he makes the best provision for our salvation, his majesty being intolerable to us if he thundered from heaven himself, this should repress the destructive itching of those who desire God daily to descend, or at least to send his revelations by angels, and who on that account despise the ministry they have. Wesley states the purpose of the terror plainly: it was a dispensation designed to make the gospel of grace the more welcome, and to be a specimen of the terrors of the judgment day.
28:
One wish of God's produces the sharpest doctrinal collision in the chapter, and both parties know they are contradicting somebody. Clarke reads it as decisive for liberty. They refuse to receive such a heart from God, and who then can supply it? If they had not been perfectly free agents, able either to use or abuse their liberty, could God have made the complaint or expressed the earnest desire we find in this verse? He made the human will free, and in spite of all the influence of sin and Satan he preserves its liberty; for had man no free will he could neither be punished nor rewarded, being a mere machine, and no more accountable for his actions than the fire for its consuming quality or the stone for its gravity — the one having burned the house of the righteous, the other having crushed the innocent to death. Calvin denies exactly this, and in those terms: this and similar passages have been ignorantly abused by some to establish man's free will, as if the will were capable of bending either way and man had the power of doing right while God without interfering looked on at the event. His own account is that God figuratively assumes a human feeling here, since it would be vain and absurd for him to desire what it is in his power to confer, having the power of bending men's hearts wherever he pleases; speaking in the character of a man, he shows that the people's perseverance was rather to be wished than hoped. And he adds the distinction on which he rests the whole: we must consider God's will as it is set before us in his word, not as it is hidden in himself, for while by his word he invites all promiscuously to life, he quickens by his secret inspiration only those whom he has elected.

Gill takes a third position, reached through the grammar. There are not properly such volitions and wishes in God, but Scripture speaks after the language of the children of men; and the words may be rendered who will give that they had such an heart — not to me, he is careful to say, but to them. From that he draws a practical conclusion neither of the others reaches: they cannot give such a heart to themselves, nor can any creature give it, and none but God can — therefore they ought to have prayed to him for a heart to hearken and do.

Calvin also gives the reason for the wish, which the others take for granted. God signifies that they would not be so firm and faithful in keeping their promises as they were ready and willing to make them, so that hypocrisy was not altogether banished or purged from their minds; and although he approves of the people's answer, he says there will be too much difficulty in the performance for the event to accord with it. Henry, who does not enter the dispute, reads the wish as evidence of what God is like: the God of heaven is truly and earnestly desirous of the welfare and salvation of poor sinners, and has given abundant proof of it — giving us time and space to repent, inviting us by his mercies, sending his Son to redeem us, publishing a general offer of pardon, and swearing that he has no pleasure in the ruin of sinners. He then turns the wish on the reader, taking it of a heart such as they had at that moment rather than such as they ought to have: it would be well with many if there were always such a heart in them as there seems to be sometimes, under conviction of sin, or the rebukes of Providence, or when they come to look death in the face.
